newRows.name: The Christian Right
newRows.statusDescription: Tiered deferred on a smaller frame (Tier 3). It was a political movement run by groups, not a church or a confession. Its public record is strong. What it formed in people's lives beyond politics is thinly recorded, and this entry says so.
newRows.sourcing: Moderate to rich. The Moral Majority's papers are kept at Liberty University. In a 1980 interview Jerry Falwell gave his own account of it. Three studies trace the whole movement, by William Martin (1996), Clyde Wilcox (1996) and Daniel K. Williams (2010).
newRows.floorNote: There is no confession of its own to test. In August 1980 Jerry Falwell said the Moral Majority was not a religious group. 'It is totally political,' he said. He counted pastors, Catholic priests, Jewish rabbis and Mormon elders among its backers. The churches its members came from are not tested through it. This reading is not settled until the later groups' own statements are checked.
newRows.relationsSummary: It grew out of the fundamentalist and evangelical churches, which have their own entries. Its groups drew support from several churches and faiths, and none became a church. They were the Moral Majority (1979–1989), the Christian Coalition (from 1989) and the Faith and Freedom Coalition (from 2009).
newRows.why: In June 1979 Jerry Falwell and four other ministers founded the Moral Majority. In August 1980 Ronald Reagan, then running for president, spoke to church leaders in Dallas. He said the gathering was nonpartisan, so it could not endorse him. Then he added, 'I endorse you and what you're doing.' The Moral Majority closed in 1989, and Pat Robertson founded the Christian Coalition that year. In 2009 Ralph Reed, the Christian Coalition's first executive director, founded the Faith and Freedom Coalition.

newRows.longDescription: Jerry Falwell, Tim LaHaye, Charles Stanley, D. James Kennedy and Greg Dixon founded the Moral Majority on 6 June 1979. It stood for four aims: pro-life, pro-family, pro-morals and pro-American. From its base in Washington, it worked in politics for those aims. In August 1980 Falwell called it 'totally political', not a religious group. Its backers, he said, were not all evangelicals. That month Ronald Reagan told church leaders in Dallas, 'I endorse you and what you're doing.' The Moral Majority closed in 1989. That same year Pat Robertson founded the Christian Coalition, with Ralph Reed as its executive director. Reed went on to found the Faith and Freedom Coalition in 2009.
newRows.teaser: In 1979 five ministers founded the Moral Majority, a political organization that drew support from several faiths.
voices: Jerry Falwell — who founded the Moral Majority with four other ministers in 1979, and called it 'totally political' in 1980
Ronald Reagan — who told church leaders in Dallas in August 1980, 'I endorse you and what you're doing'
Pat Robertson — who founded the Christian Coalition in 1989
Ralph Reed — the Christian Coalition's first executive director, who founded the Faith and Freedom Coalition in 2009
William Martin — whose With God on Our Side (1996) told the story of the movement's rise
newRows.legacy: Its groups changed over thirty years, but the movement carried on. In 2010 the historian Daniel K. Williams told its story in God's Own Party. The record shows its political work well. It shows much less of what the movement meant for its members' faith.

livingEvidence.basis: A current, a label or a skeleton; the flag is a judgment on the evidence. One carrier, the Faith and Freedom Coalition, still meets in a yearly conference.
livingEvidence.evidence: Andrew R. Lewis, The Rights Turn in Conservative Christian Politics (Cambridge University Press, 2017): independent scholarship; verified. Washington Examiner, on the Faith & Freedom Coalition's Road to Majority conference (26-28 June 2025): independent news; verified, the article's own date not seen.
